title: The Pistons Should Go for It
contentHtml:
Another way I would like to use this space: talking about a big game that lands in the dead zone between podcast episodes.

You never want to read too much into any one regular-season win, but the Detroit Pistons going to San Antonio and stomping out the Spurs’ 12-game win streak—despite missing two starters and two rotation reserves—was a capital-letter Regular-Season Win. It was a proof of concept: When we do what we do well, with calculated force, we can drag even the best into our style of play and do some real damage. (The Spurs, admittedly, did not play a great game on offense.)

The nagging thought in my head the entire game, and since: Detroit should go for it.

Cade Cunningham is ready, now, at age 25. As Kirk Goldsberry wrote earlier this month, the NBA is getting younger. Front offices should at least tweak their traditional “journey to title contention” schedules. An ultra-young team nearly won the whole thing last season, and sure, they have Victor Wembanyama, and sure, San Antonio’s inexperience derailed them in crunch time in the Finals, but teams shouldn’t necessarily wait until their best players are 27-plus to really push in.

It’s not as if the Pistons are postseason neophytes, either—even if they are only two-plus calendar years removed from one of the most embarrassing seasons in franchise history, a 14-68 pratfall that featured a 28-game losing streak. Two seasons ago, they pushed a very good New York Knicks team six games in the first round. Last season, they trudged past the Orlando Magic in seven games before losing Game 7 at home in the conference semifinals to the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Last year’s Pistons played it conservative at the trade deadline, striking a small deal for Kevin Huerter—who barely factored into their postseason run due to a groin injury but is playing quite well this season. Caution was justifiable, even with Detroit standing atop an underwhelming East. The Pistons wanted to see how their young cornerstones fared under the pressure of expectations and whether—and how—concerns about their offensive spacing would really manifest in the playoffs.

A year later, the East, again, does not look like the 11-deep murderer’s row a lot of us (guilty) anticipated. That could change as revamped teams in Miami, Philadelphia, and Boston jell and as key players get healthy: Tyrese Haliburton, Kawhi Leonard, Paolo Banchero. (For those keeping score: The Toronto 2.0 era has brought more awkward team statements on Leonard’s return from this “please don’t call it an injury” injury—three—than Leonard games played—two.)

Every chance at true title contention is precious. Injuries and bad luck can undo teams that look poised for dynastic runs.

The case against Detroit getting too aggressive is pretty simple, and similar to the case you might have made last season:

  • Jalen Duren and Ausar Thompson are both just 23, and as of today, we aren’t much closer than we were a month ago to learning how the Pistons will build a functional postseason offense with those two sharing the floor for half of every game.

  • Last year’s Pistons (probably) would have lost in the first round had Franz Wagner not gotten injured. Maybe this team needs more time and seasoning before the brass should be aggressive.

  • The Pistons are expensive, having locked Duren and Thompson into big extensions alongside Cunningham’s max deal; taking on a fourth big long-term salary could be unwieldy, and trading away picks to do it would hamstring Detroit’s ability to churn the middle and back of the roster with cheaper salaries. They are already facing Daniss Jenkins’s restricted free agency this summer.

All fair! I’m not necessarily suggesting Detroit break the bank here! But a lot of variables might be lining up to put Detroit in a favorable buy-now position.
